beats.narration_text: Namaste — this is Liam, in for Ameya. Build it with Claude, then take it apart. If someone asks you how a RAG system really works, here are the answers that actually matter — the standard pipeline, and the handful of truths that move quality more than anything else.

props.command: claude "give me the RAG answers that actually matter — the standard pipeline and the truths that move quality"
props.topic: CLAUDE CODE · RAG, THE FIELD STANDARD
output: chunk & hybrid retrieval move quality most

beats.narration_text: Start with the shape everyone shares. Ingest, chunk, embed, index, retrieve, optionally rerank, then augment the prompt and generate. And three maturity levels: naive just stuffs the top matches in; advanced adds query rewriting and reranking; agentic lets the model decide when to retrieve at all.
beats.visual_intent: horizontal pipeline: ingest→chunk→embed→index→retrieve→(rerank)→augment→generate; below: naive / advanced / agentic tiers

beats.narration_text: Chunking first, because it moves quality more than most people expect. Recursive splitting is the production default — try paragraphs, then lines, then sentences. Start around two-to-five-hundred tokens with ten to twenty percent overlap. And when small chunks retrieve well but lack context, index the small ones and return their larger parent.
beats.visual_intent: chunking table: fixed / recursive (default) / document / semantic / parent-document; '256-512 tokens, 10-20% overlap'

beats.narration_text: Embeddings come in two shapes, and the difference is the whole game. A bi-encoder encodes the query and the document separately, so document vectors precompute — that's your fast first-stage retrieval. A cross-encoder reads both together: far more accurate, impossible to precompute. So it reranks a shortlist; it never retrieves. Normalize once, and cosine similarity becomes a plain dot product.
beats.visual_intent: two panels: bi-encoder (separate, precompute, fast, retrieve) vs cross-encoder (together, accurate, rerank only); normalize→dot note

beats.narration_text: Under the vector database, four choices. Flat compares against everything — exact, fine up to about a hundred thousand. HNSW walks a proximity graph — fast and high-recall, but memory hungry. IVF searches only the nearest clusters. Quantization compresses the vectors to save memory. The one line to say out loud: it's recall versus latency versus memory. Approximate search buys speed by giving up exactness.
beats.visual_intent: index table Flat/HNSW/IVF/PQ; triangle: recall — latency — memory

beats.narration_text: Then hybrid search — usually the biggest quality win after chunking. Keyword search, BM25, nails exact terms: names, product codes, rare tokens. Dense embeddings catch meaning and paraphrase. Each fails where the other shines, so you run both and fuse the ranked lists with reciprocal rank fusion — no calibrated scores required.
beats.visual_intent: sparse (BM25: exact terms) + dense (embeddings: meaning) → RRF fusion → merged ranking

beats.narration_text: When you need more, a toolbox sits before and after retrieval. Query rewriting cleans up a messy question. HyDE writes a hypothetical answer and searches with that. Reranking re-scores the shortlist with a cross-encoder. And contextual retrieval prepends a short summary of the parent document to each chunk before embedding. Small moves, real gains.
beats.visual_intent: 2x2 grid of technique chips: query rewriting, HyDE, reranking, contextual retrieval (+ self-query, compression)

beats.narration_text: Now the part interviewers probe hardest: how do you know it works. Split it in two. Retrieval quality — hit rate, MRR, NDCG — did you find the right context. Generation quality — faithfulness, relevance, correctness — did the answer stay grounded in it. Debug retrieval first, always. If the context is wrong, no prompt saves the answer.
beats.visual_intent: two columns: RETRIEVAL (hit@k, MRR, NDCG) | GENERATION (faithfulness, relevance, correctness); 'debug retrieval first'

beats.narration_text: You'll reach for a language model as the judge — it's cheap and it scales. Just know its tells: it favours the first option, it favours longer answers, and it favours its own family. Randomize the order, give it a rubric, and check it against human labels before you trust it. Validate the judge before you trust the judge.
beats.visual_intent: three bias chips: position bias / verbosity bias / self-preference; mitigations; big line 'validate the judge before you trust the judge'

beats.narration_text: In production, four levers. Latency — stream the first token so it feels fast. Cost — input tokens dominate, so route by difficulty and trim the context. Caching — an exact match is instant, and a semantic cache catches near-duplicate questions. Guardrails — validate the input, check the answer is grounded, and shape the output as real structure, not parsed prose.
beats.visual_intent: four cards: latency (TTFT/stream) · cost (input tokens, routing) · cache (exact + semantic) · guardrails (grounding, schema)

beats.narration_text: One last thing, and it's the most useful. When you're asked about something you haven't built, the strong answer is simple: I haven't done that in production; my understanding is this; if I were starting, I'd do that. That's credible. Bluffing is the only version that loses.
beats.visual_intent: the honest-framing template as three lines; a couple of one-liners underneath

beats.narration_text: So if you keep three things: chunking and hybrid retrieval move quality more than swapping embedding models. A cross-encoder is a reranker, never a retriever. And validate the judge before you trust the judge. Get those right and the rest is tuning.

artifactLines: Chunking + hybrid retrieval beat swapping embedding models.
A cross-encoder reranks a shortlist — it never retrieves.
Validate the judge before you trust the judge.

beats.role_note: HANDOFF LAW — prompt read + discussed; 'Your turn.'
beats.narration_text: Your turn. Take this prompt and point it at your own system: build a small golden set from real questions, then measure retrieval and generation separately so you can see which half is failing. Once you can see it, you can fix it — and you'll have a real answer for any interview, because you'll have done it.
